evidence_quote: to be eligible for Higher Achievement, students and their parents needed to complete an application, attend an in-person interview and commit to active participation for three to four years.
resolved_title: Staying On Track: Testing Higher Achievement's Long-Term Impact on Academic Outcomes and High School Choice
notes: Lottery among 952 applicants (rising 5th and 6th graders) to five Higher Achievement centers in DC and Alexandria, so universal with opt_in = 1 per the codebook. No achievement or income rule at the student level; applicants scored slightly above the national average and 60 percent were FRL. Caveat: the program sites its centers in 'at-risk communities' and recruits mainly through school referrals, which a reviewer could read as targeted_other at the site level; coded on the applicant lottery rule and confidence set to medium for that reason. Kraft n 719 to 815 fits the follow-up analytic samples. | adjudication: Rule (Andrew, 2026-09-25): lottery applicants to a program that serves a needy area or population are targeted_other. Higher Achievement sites its centers in at-risk communities, so the selection is at site level.

evidence_quote: The 32 school leaders who volunteered to join the experimental sample represented a diverse array of elementary schools in terms of prior achievement, demographics, and geography.
resolved_title: The Impact of Achieve3000 on Elementary Literacy Outcomes: Randomized Control Trial Evidence, 2013-14 to 2014-15 (WCPSS DRA Report No. 16.02)
notes: Wake County elementary schools were eligible after removing the 12 pilot schools and SuccessMaker schools; 32 volunteering schools were paired on 2013 reading composites and randomized (16 treatment, 16 control); all students in grades 2 to 5 in those schools were in the sample. Volunteering is not selection on need (tie-breaker 6). Kraft n 6235 to 12851 fits the annual and pooled analytic samples. Not in the WWC export; manual match accepted WWC study 85405, the same DRA report.

evidence_quote: Pupils were eligible as long as they were in the bottom 15-20% of mathematics achievement based on attainment at KS1, as well as the professional judgement of teachers based on their more recent performance.
resolved_title: Catch Up Numeracy: Evaluation report and executive summary (Hodgen, Adkins, Ainsworth, and Evans, 2019, EEF)
notes: Schools recruited by the developer had to provide at least six eligible Year 4 and six eligible Year 5 pupils (or four in each of Years 3 to 5); that is a capacity requirement, not school selection on need, so level is student. Kraft n 1481 matches the primary model and n 551 the everFSM subgroup (summary table PDF p. 5), so one of the two effects is a subgroup. Report notes schools interpreted the eligibility criterion broadly.

evidence_quote: All participating schools met the following criteria for inclusion in the project: (a) is an elementary school; (b) has been implementing positive behavioral interventions and supports (PBIS) for at least 1 year, as documented by district records
resolved_title: A Randomized Waitlist Controlled Analysis of Team-Initiated Problem Solving Professional Development and Use
notes: Thirty-eight K-5 schools in North Carolina and Oregon, recruited as a convenience sample of schools already implementing PBIS and using SWIS with a monthly team meeting; criteria are implementation features, not need or achievement (tie-breaker 6). All students in the schools are the student sample. Kraft n 2765 to 2984 is far below the WWC full sample of 18,443 students, so Kraft's math effects may come from a grade-level subsample or a companion report; the journal article itself reports team-process outcomes, and the student achievement results are not described in this text.

evidence_quote: Specifically, if a charter school in New York receives more applicants than it has places, it must hold a random lottery among the applicants. Lotteries are specific to a school, grade, and year of intended entry
resolved_title: Charter Schools in New York City: Who Enrolls and How They Affect Their Students' Achievement (NBER Working Paper 14852, 2009)
notes: Lotteried-in versus lotteried-out applicants to NYC charter schools, tests in grades 3-8; no applicant eligibility rule beyond applying. Text is the NBER working paper. Kraft n 32551 not checked against the paper's tables.

evidence_quote: The target cohort within the schools were pupils in Year 4 (Y4) and Year 5 (Y5) in the first year of the trial (2016/2017). After accounting for parental/carer opt-outs (n = 117; 0.91%), this sample consisted of n = 6,586 and n = 6,338 pupils in the Y4 and Y5 cohorts, respectively.
resolved_title: Achievement for All Evaluation Report (Humphrey, Squires, Choudry, Byrne, Demkowicz, Troncoso, and Wo, 2020, EEF)
notes: Whole-school programme; 134 schools recruited by the developer (only rule: not previously involved with AfA) and randomised; all Y5 pupils analysed. Schools nominated a 20 percent AfA target group of vulnerable pupils, but the headline analysis is the whole cohort. Kraft n 5813 is the complete-case whole-cohort KS2 reading sample and n 1231 the FSM subgroup (ES -0.157 in the FSM table), so one of the two effects is a subgroup. Hand-supplied PDF.

evidence_quote: The parents of all pupils in Years 3 to 6 of the 16 recruited schools were invited to take part in the intervention. Of those, 2,690 pupils in 2,306 distinct families did not opt out.
resolved_title: Parent Academy: Evaluation report and executive summary (Husain, Jabin, Haywood, Kasim, and Paylor, 2016, EEF)
notes: Pupil-level randomisation among all Years 3 to 6 pupils whose parents did not opt out, in 16 schools recruited on a convenience basis in two local authorities; intention to treat, so opt_in 0 even though parents chose whether to attend the academy. Kraft n 1465-1578 does not match the report analysed samples of 1,895 (reading) and 1,923 (maths); the four Kraft effects may include the FSM-only analysis or the adjusted models. No achievement rule.

evidence_quote: District selection was based upon factors such as district size and poverty ... The selected districts, which were spread across 13 states, served low-income students, with every district in the study having more than 50 percent of its students qualifying for the federal School Lunch Program.
resolved_title: Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Results from the Second Year of a Randomized Controlled Study (NCEE 2009-4072)
notes: Districts chosen partly on poverty; within districts, all beginning K-6 teachers in the study schools and their students, no student rule. Kraft n 3000 does not match any report sample (one-year districts 1,917 reading and 1,683 math students, p. 34; two-year districts 1,303 and 1,242); possibly a sum or a rounded figure.

evidence_quote: We worked with HMH to recruit 12 schools with grades 3, 4, and 5. We randomized intact grade-level teams that volunteered for participation to the MIF and control groups.
resolved_title: Assessing Impacts of Math in Focus, a 'Singapore Math' Program for American Schools
notes: SREE 2015 abstract (ED562089) of the 2016 JREE article; one urban Nevada district. Grade-level teams volunteered (tie-breaker 6); no student rule. Kraft n 1,641 is an analytic sample of the 2,235 rostered students. Data flags: Kraft's grade span 3-5,9-12 is wrong (grades 3 to 5 only), and the WWC row attached to 432 is Newman et al. (Alabama AMSTI), a different study.

evidence_quote: At the start of the school year, schools and Reading Partners staff developed a list of students who were deemed eligible for Reading Partners based on a combination of test score review and teacher and/or staff recommendation.
resolved_title: Leveraging Volunteers: An Experimental Evaluation of a Tutoring Program for Struggling Readers
notes: Reading Partners volunteer tutoring; 1,657 students recruited, 1,265 consented, randomized within school and grade group (p. 8); parental consent was required for the pull-out tutoring, hence opt_in 1. Schools were 89 percent Title I but were recruited as existing program sites, not selected on Title I (p. 9). Kraft n 1,166 is the analytic sample.

evidence_quote: At each site, teachers, principals, and reading specialists identify students who are reading below grade level and consider the different reading interventions that are available to students.
resolved_title: Mobilizing Volunteer Tutors to Improve Student Literacy: Implementation, Impacts, and Costs of the Reading Partners Program (MDRC, March 2015)
notes: Students in grades 2 to 5 were referred to Reading Partners by school staff for reading below grade level, then randomized within school (1,265 students, 19 schools); all had parental consent for the pull-out tutoring study, so opt_in = 1 per the codebook. Schools were established Reading Partners sites in under-resourced, mostly schoolwide Title I schools with more capacity demand than seats, so level = both. Kraft n 492 to 1147 matches the WWC all-student and grade-band samples.

evidence_quote: Subjects: A total of 2,308 elementary students eligible for and interested in attending a 21st Century Community Learning Center. A total of 973 students applied to 18 centers in fall 2000, and 1,335 applied to 8 centers in fall 2001.
resolved_title: When Schools Stay Open Late: The National Evaluation of the 21st Century Community Learning Centers Program: Final Report (2005)
notes: Applicants to oversubscribed after-school centers were randomized (p. 34). Centers were chosen for oversubscription, and the report describes the program as serving mostly low-income schools, but no student selection rule beyond applying. Kraft n 2308 matches.

evidence_quote: Eligible schools were those having at least two Year 5 classes and a high proportion (over 20%) of children eligible for free school meals (FSM pupils).
resolved_title: Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation report and executive summary (Jay et al., 2017, EEF)
notes: 78 schools in Leeds, Bradford, and Birmingham recruited on an FSM threshold and randomised; all Year 5 pupils in the schools took part. Analysed sample was 1,832 intervention and 2,080 control pupils, so Kraft n 603-1239 does not match the full sample; 1,239 and 603 appear in secondary-outcome and subgroup tables, so Kraft effects appear to come from subsamples.

evidence_quote: This paper attempts to overcome these limitations by presenting evidence from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving more than 4,000 children in England.
resolved_title: Does Teaching Children How to Play Cognitively Demanding Games Improve Their Educational Attainment? (Jerrim, Macmillan, Micklewright, Sawtell, and Wiggins, 2018, Journal of Human Resources)
notes: Abstract only; it gives no sample description beyond the count, so no eligibility rule can be read. Kraft cites the 2016 EEF Chess in Schools evaluation report by the same authors; the resolved item is the later journal version of the same trial. Kraft n 1321 does not match the abstract's more than 4,000 children. Study 995 was resolved to this same abstract but appears to be a different trial (see its note).

No document exists (retrieval status unresolved). The BEE elementary math table gives 139 teachers, 1,897 students, grades 2 and 4, University of Cincinnati evaluation; the eligibility rule is not stated in anything available.

evidence_quote: Subjects for this study were third, fourth, and fifth grade students in the Derry Township School District in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Derry Township is a small district with approximately 2,500 students in a wealthy community where the average I.Q. is 118.
resolved_title: The Effectiveness of Team Accelerated Instruction on High Achievers in Mathematics
notes: The district was chosen to study high achievers ('a district where achievement is already above average', p. 1), so selection on a characteristic at the district level; all students in 12 classrooms, no student rule. Students were randomly assigned to classrooms and two classes per grade were taught with TAI, not a lottery on treatment. Data flags: the article reports 247 students (34 and 35, 44 and 44, 46 and 44 across grades 3 to 5), not Kraft's n 588, and Kraft's grade span 3-12 is wrong (grades 3 to 5). Text is the EBSCO full text.

evidence_quote: This reports focuses on a sample of 1,764 students (referred to in this report as the study sample) who applied for one of the Career Academies selected for the study.
resolved_title: Career Academies: Impacts on Students' Engagement and Performance in High School (MDRC, 2000)
notes: Lottery among applicants identified in grade 8 or 9. MDRC's interest in at-risk students (p. 19) is motivation, not a sample rule (tie-breaker 7). Kraft n 1764 matches the study sample, but the standardized achievement test was given to a 490-student subsample (p. 20), so Kraft's test-score effects likely rest on that subsample, hence mixed_samples 1. wwc-codes row describes a 1,482-student grade 9-12 sample.

evidence_quote: The effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention with and without a parent training component were evaluated with a sample of low-income Latino children from language minority families.
resolved_title: The efficacy of a voluntary summer book reading intervention for low-income Latino children from language minority families
notes: The sample is defined by low-income, Latino, language-minority status (title and abstract), but the abstract does not say whether this operated by choosing schools or screening students, so level unclear. Children were pretested in school and randomized; 'voluntary' describes the summer reading, not enrollment. Data flag: Kraft lists the subject as Math with n 317; the outcomes are reading comprehension and vocabulary (370 randomized).

evidence_quote: A total of 24 teachers and 400 children in Grades 3, 4, and 5 were randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions: control, books only, books with oral reading scaffolding, and books with oral reading and comprehension scaffolding.
resolved_title: Scaffolding Voluntary Summer Reading for Children in Grades 3 to 5: An Experimental Study
notes: No eligibility rule stated. Kraft n 400 matches.

evidence_quote: The effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention were assessed in a randomized field trial involving 552 students in 10 schools. In this study, fourth-grade children received eight books to read during their summer vacation
resolved_title: Effects of a Voluntary Summer Reading Intervention on Reading Achievement: Results From a Randomized Field Trial
notes: No eligibility rule stated; subgroup effects for less fluent readers are reported but Kraft's 0.02 is an overall estimate. Kraft n 486 is an analytic sample of 552.

evidence_quote: A total of 24 teachers and 400 children in Grades 3, 4, and 5 were randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions: control, books only, books with oral reading scaffolding, and books with oral reading and comprehension scaffolding.
resolved_title: Scaffolding Voluntary Summer Reading for Children in Grades 3 to 5: An Experimental Study (Kim and White, 2008, Scientific Studies of Reading)
notes: Abstract only. Children in the classrooms of 24 teachers randomised across four conditions; no achievement or demographic rule stated, and the abstract does not say whether every child in those classrooms was included. Voluntary refers to the summer reading, not to enrolment in the study, so opt_in 0. Kraft n 400 matches. Confidence capped at medium by the abstract-only rule.

evidence_quote: A total of 294 children in Grades 4–6 were randomly assigned to READ 180 or a district after-school program.
resolved_title: A randomized experiment of a mixed-methods literacy intervention for struggling readers in grades 4-6: effects on word reading efficiency, reading comprehension and vocabulary, and oral reading fluency
notes: Same after-school READ 180 Enterprise trial as 483-kim-2011 (EEPA), whose abstract states the rule: fourth to sixth graders reading below proficiency on the state assessment at baseline, enrolled in an after-school program (opt_in 1). Coded identically with 483 as its twin; this abstract names struggling readers only in the title. Kraft n 264 fits an analytic subset of 294.

evidence_quote: In this randomized controlled trial involving 312 students enrolled in an after-school program, the authors generated intention-to-treat and treatment-on-the-treated estimates of the program’s impact on several literacy outcomes of fourth, fifth, and sixth graders reading below proficiency on a state assessment at baseline.
resolved_title: Can a Mixed-Method Literacy Intervention Improve the Reading Achievement of Low-Performing Elementary School Students in an After-School Program? Results From a Randomized Controlled Trial of READ 180 Enterprise
notes: Twin of 482-kim-2010 (same trial, Reading and Writing 2010 article). Data flags: the WWC row attached to 483 is the Pathway Project (Kim, Olson, et al. 2011, Santa Ana English learners), which belongs to 485-olson-2012, not this READ 180 study; the codebook's worked example for key 483-kim-2011 describes that Pathway sample and so applies to 485. Kraft n 306 fits 312 randomized.

evidence_quote: The study examined the impact of the Pathway Project intervention on students who were mainstreamed Latino English language learners (ELLs). One hundred and three English teachers in 15 schools in California were recruited and randomly assigned
resolved_title: WWC Review of the Report: A Randomized Experiment of a Cognitive Strategies Approach to Text-Based Analytical Writing for Mainstreamed Latino English Language Learners in Grades 6 to 12
notes: text/484-kim-2011.txt is the WWC single study review (August 2012) of Kim et al. 2011, not the JREE article, so confidence is medium. Same trial as the codebook's worked example 483-kim-2011 (another batch), which should carry the same code. Kraft's n_max 4,459 and grade span 4-11 do not match the article (2,726 students, grades 6-12); resolution note says 4,459 is the BEE pooled two-cohort figure.

evidence_quote: The sample included 2,726 English learner students in grades 6 to 12. All students were English learners, 95% of students were Hispanic, and Spanish was the first language for 88% of students.
resolved_title: Enhancing the Interpretive Reading and Analytical Writing of Mainstreamed English Learners in Secondary School
notes: The abstract (title and text: mainstreamed English learners, 72 Santa Ana teachers randomized) and the WWC sample text agree, so confidence medium rather than low. Kraft n 4,459 is plausible for the two-year sample; the WWC-reviewed sample is 2,726. Kraft's 0.48 is the on-demand writing assessment and 0.10 the standardized writing test.

evidence_quote: This study examined the efficacy of a supplemental, multicomponent adolescent reading intervention for middle school students who scored below proficient on a state literacy assessment.
resolved_title: Engaging Struggling Adolescent Readers to Improve Reading Skills
notes: WWC sample text agrees: 483 eligible students identified as needing intensive reading support on the state ELA test, excluding separate special education classes and beginning ELLs. All eight schools were Title I but no school selection rule is stated, so level student. Kraft n 398 is an analytic sample of 483.

evidence_quote: The effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention were assessed in a randomized field trial involving 552 students in 10 schools. In this study, fourth-grade children received eight books to read during their summer vacation
resolved_title: Effects of a Voluntary Summer Reading Intervention on Reading Achievement: Results From a Randomized Field Trial (EEPA, 2006)
notes: Voluntary describes the summer reading, not enrollment; fourth graders in 10 schools with no student rule stated. Subgroup effects reported for Black, Latino, and less fluent readers, but Kraft's 0.01 is consistent with an overall effect. Kraft n 552 matches.

evidence_quote: The causal effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention on children's reading activities and reading achievement were assessed in a randomized experiment involving 331 children in Grades 1-5.
resolved_title: The effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention on reading activities and reading achievement (Journal of Educational Psychology, 2007, 99(3), 505-515)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: the abstract (ERIC EJ772024, DOI 10.1037/0022-0663.99.3.505) is the correct article, Kim 2007, and Kraft's n 331 matches; no open full text was found. The abstract states no school or student eligibility rule: children were pretested, stratified by grade and classroom, and randomized to receive 10 matched books over the summer. The word voluntary describes the summer reading, not enrollment, and nothing describes an application, so opt_in 0. Because the abstract does not say whether all children in the participating classrooms took part or how the site was chosen, the code is unclear rather than universal.

evidence_quote: The current study examines whether Word Generation (WG), a Tier-I discussion-based program designed to build academic literacy and linguistic practices, provides differential gains for non-ELL and ELL students
resolved_title: Reducing academic inequalities for English language learners: Variation in experimental effects of Word Generation in high-poverty schools
notes: DATA PROBLEM: the WWC row (85771) is Kim, Hemphill, Troyer et al. 2017 on STARI (grades 6 to 8, about 400 students), not the Kim, Hsin, and Snow 2018 Word Generation paper Kraft cites (n 2160 to 2226, grades 4 to 7); the WWC match is wrong and its sample text was not used. The abstract describes a universal Tier-I program in high-poverty schools but never states how schools or students were selected, so unclear. Kraft's two effects (0.03, 0.03) may be full-sample reading comprehension estimates by year or ELL versus non-ELL subgroup estimates; cannot tell from the abstract. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: In this randomized controlled trial involving 312 students enrolled in an after-school program, the authors generated intention-to-treat and treatment-on-the-treated estimates of the program's impact on several literacy outcomes of fourth, fifth, and sixth graders reading below proficiency on a state assessment at baseline.
resolved_title: Can a mixed-method literacy intervention improve the reading achievement of low-performing elementary school students in an after-school program? Results from a randomized controlled trial of READ 180 Enterprise
notes: Students enrolled in an after-school program (opt_in) and were reading below proficiency on the MCAS at baseline; the WWC text says 95 percent, not all, scored below proficiency, so the rule was not a strict cutoff. This is the Cohort 1 first-year sample (297 students per WWC) of the Brockton READ 180 trial also reported in 284-fitzgerald-2008 and 494-kim-2010. Kraft n 296 matches the WWC full sample. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: Students who were identified as English language learners (ELLs) and were eligible for mainstreaming were randomly assigned to classrooms participating in the study.
resolved_title: WWC Review of the Report: A Randomized Experiment of a Cognitive Strategies Approach to Text-Based Analytical Writing for Mainstreamed Latino English Language Learners in Grades 6 to 12
notes: DATA NOTE: text/493-kim-2011.txt is the WWC single study review (August 2012) of the Kim, Olson et al. 2011 JREE article, not the article itself, so confidence is medium. All 2,726 students were English learners eligible for mainstreaming in Santa Ana USD; selection on ELL status, not on a score. Kraft n 1393 to 2721 matches the WWC analysis samples. The codebook worked example 483-kim-2011 (another batch) is the same Pathway Project study, so rows 483 and 493 look like a cross-batch twin; codes should match.

evidence_quote: administered during an hour-long after-school program to groups of randomly selected students in grades 4-6 who were identified as struggling readers prior to randomization
resolved_title: A randomized experiment of a mixed-methods literacy intervention for struggling readers in grades 4-6: Effects on word reading efficiency, reading comprehension and vocabulary, and oral reading fluency
notes: The abstract (ERIC) states only that 294 children in grades 4 to 6 were randomly assigned to READ 180 or a district after-school program; the title and the WWC setting text both say the students were struggling readers identified before randomization, so the two sources agree and confidence is medium rather than low. After-school program implies enrollment (opt_in). Second-year combined-cohort sample of the Brockton READ 180 trial (see 284-fitzgerald-2008, 491-kim-2011). Kraft n 264 matches the WWC full analytic sample.

evidence_quote: We use high-quality data from a large-scale school-level cluster randomized experiment to examine the impact of two well-known commercial interim assessment programs on mathematics and reading achievement in Indiana.
resolved_title: The Impact of Indiana's System of Interim Assessments on Mathematics and Reading Achievement
notes: Abstract only (Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, paywalled); it names the design and state but no school or student eligibility rule, and no WWC sample text exists for this study. Kraft's n 11,623 to 20,000 could not be checked.

evidence_quote: We use data from a large-scale, school-level randomized experiment conducted in 2010-2011 in public schools in Indiana. Our sample includes more than 30,000 students in 70 schools.
resolved_title: Effects of Interim Assessments on Student Achievement: Evidence From a Large-Scale Experiment (Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 2016)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: the abstract (ERIC EJ1115334, DOI 10.1080/19345747.2015.1116031) is the correct article, Konstantopoulos, Li, Miller, and van der Ploeg 2016; no open full text was found. Seventy Indiana public schools were randomized to interim assessment programs (mCLASS in K-2, Acuity in 3-8) serving all students in the school, and the abstract states no need-based rule for schools; coded universal on the Festas precedent in codebook section 6, with medium confidence because the abstract does not say how the 70 schools were recruited. Kraft's n 13,944 is presumably the grade 3-8 Acuity math sample; Kraft's grades_all K-6 differs from the abstract's K-8.

evidence_quote: The study was conducted in one school district and involved 76 teachers and their classes in grades 3 to 6. Within each grade level, half the teachers were randomly assigned to the treatment group and half were randomly assigned to the control group.
resolved_title: Experimental Study on the Impact of the 6+1 Trait Writing Model on Student Achievement in Writing
notes: Writing outcome (6+1 Trait), listed by Kraft under reading. No selection rule for the district or students is stated; low-poverty sample (10 percent FRPL, under 1 percent ELL or minority). Kraft n 1,592 matches the students with complete data.

evidence_quote: Middle school students (N = 5,870) from diverse backgrounds participated in a randomized study of the intervention that was conducted in 12 middle schools located in an urban school district.
resolved_title: Assessing Adolescents' Communicative Self-Efficacy to Discuss Controversial Issues: Findings From a Randomized Study of the Word Generation Program
notes: Per the header note in the abstract file, Kraft's reading effects (0.07, 0.00, 0.05; n 8,466) come from the Word Generation trial via the BEE table, not from this self-efficacy article, so mixed_samples 1 and confidence low. No eligibility rule beyond school membership is stated.

recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: retrieval status failed; no open copy and no abstract of Lenard and Rhea 2019 (DreamBox Learning, Wake County; Kraft n 12,467, grades K-5, math ES 0.08) exists in text/ or abstracts/, and wwc-codes.csv has no row for this study, so no document was read and the code is unclear with no source, per the batch instructions.

evidence_quote: The study, which incorporated multi-site cluster-randomized design, was conducted in four middle schools with 2,150 students and 47 teachers.
resolved_title: Effects of Differentiated Reading Instruction on Student Achievement in Middle School
notes: Differentiated reading for whole classes; no student rule stated. Kraft n 2,028 is an analytic sample of 2,150.

evidence_quote: Ten secondary schools in North East England were recruited to take part in the trial, selecting schools where the proportion of pupils eligible for free school meals (FSM) was above the national average.
resolved_title: Paired Reading: Evaluation report and Executive summary (Lloyd, Edovald, Kiss, Morris, Skipp, and Ahmed, 2015, EEF)
notes: Class-level randomisation; all Year 7 (tutee) and Year 9 (tutor) classes in the schools were eligible, with extra classes dropped only to equalise numbers. Kraft n 1300 (Year 7) and 1265 (Year 9) match the adjusted analyses. The wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is a different study (Kennedy, Deshler, and Lloyd 2015) and was ignored. UK Years 7 and 9 are US grades 6 and 8.

evidence_quote: it was intended that around 40 per cent of schools in the study sample were to be or have been below the government performance floor target threshold at some time in the last three years ... The local authorities were asked to prioritise schools that were perceived as having weaknesses in maths teaching
resolved_title: Durham Shared Maths Project: Evaluation report and Executive summary (Lloyd, Edovald, Morris, Kiss, Skipp, and Haywood, 2015, EEF)
notes: Cluster RCT in 82 schools across four local authorities; all Year 3 and Year 5 pupils in recruited schools took part, so any selection is at school level. Recruitment aims were that about 40 percent of schools be below the floor target and that schools come from high-deprivation areas, and local authorities were asked to prioritise schools with perceived weaknesses in maths teaching; these were aims, not strict criteria, so confidence is medium and a reviewer could prefer targeted_other (deprivation) or universal. Kraft n 2786 (Year 5) and 2683 (Year 3) match the analysed samples. Hand-supplied PDF; the wwc-codes.csv row for this study_id is a different study (Kennedy et al. 2015). | adjudication: Rule (Andrew, 2026-09-25): recruitment that focused on, preferentially targeted, or aimed at poor or low-performing districts or schools counts as targeted even without a strict criterion. Low achievement plus poverty is targeted_low (tie-breaker 1). Confirms coder's value.

evidence_quote: Children in Years 3, 4 and 5 on a given school's full-time roll at the start of the 2012-13 academic year were the target population for the study.
resolved_title: Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS): Evaluation report and Executive summary
notes: EEF cluster RCT, 45 mainstream primary schools in Greater Manchester, England; eligibility was any mainstream primary school in the 10 Greater Manchester local authorities (p. 10), no pupil rule. Kraft n 2699 matches the BEE listing of the Years 5-6 Key Stage 2 maths sample. International setting.
No source: retrieval status unresolved for Madden et al., 2011; no full text, abstract, or WWC sample text exists, so no eligibility rule can be read.

evidence_quote: To be eligible to participate, schools had to be part of the NYCDOE public school system and have an existing arts program in at least one arts discipline. ... Two informational meetings in winter 2011 were held to describe the program and to recruit volunteer schools to participate in the study.
resolved_title: Arts Achieve, Impacting Student Success in the Arts: Preliminary Findings After One Year of Implementation
notes: Volunteer NYC schools with existing arts programs; classes chosen by grade (grade 5, 8, and a high school grade) and whole classes were tested. No need-based rule at any level.

evidence_quote: To be eligible for a scholarship, children had to be entering grades one through five, living in New York City, attending a public school at the time of application, and be a member of a family with an income that qualified children for the federal School Lunch Program.
resolved_title: School Choice in New York City After Three Years: An Evaluation of the School Choice Scholarships Program: Final Report (Mathematica, 2002)
notes: Income-eligible applicants randomized by lottery. 85 percent of scholarships were reserved for applicants from public schools with below-median test scores (p. 12); that is a school-level performance weight in the lottery, not an eligibility rule, and estimates are weighted back to all eligible applicants. Kraft n 1960 not verified in text.

evidence_quote: Analyzes the impact of a negative income tax experiment on the school performance of children in grades 4 through 10
resolved_title: The Effects of a Negative Income Tax on School Performance: Results of an Experiment (Journal of Human Resources, 1979)
notes: Abstract gives no eligibility rule. Families in a negative income tax experiment are enrolled by income, which would make this targeted_other at the family level with opt_in 1 if the full text confirms it. Kraft n 851 not verifiable. | adjudication: Rule (Andrew, 2026-09-25): lottery applicants to a program that serves a needy area or population are targeted_other. Negative income tax experiment; families enrolled on income.

evidence_quote: The cut-off scores for student eligibility were set by Newark Public Schools (NPS), based on one standard deviation from the norm.
resolved_title: Striving Readers Study: Targeted and Whole-School Interventions, Year 5 (Westat, 2011)
notes: Newark Striving Readers. School rule: Title I eligible middle schools designated in need of improvement under NCLB, not already using READ 180 (report p. 5); 19 schools randomized. Student rule for the targeted READ 180 evaluation: NJASK reading subtest score below a district cut-off about one SD below the norm, that is, reading well below grade level. Kraft's 29 effects with n 436 to 2555 appear to mix the targeted sample (hundreds per grade or year) and the whole-school sample (all students in study schools), so mixed_samples = 1; both samples are targeted_low (student rule for targeted, INOI school rule for whole-school). Manual WWC match accepted 81694. Long report; read the executive summary and section 3.A only.

evidence_quote: Schools were eligible to participate in the project if they were a mainstream state secondary school in any area of England willing to be randomised to implementing the intervention (and pay a contribution of 10,000 pounds) or to be part of a business as usual control group.
